## The big idea

Divide the energy balance by $\rho g$ and every term becomes a **height**:
the head equation. It is Bernoulli grown up — same three currencies, plus
a term for head *added* ($H_a$, pumps), head *extracted* ($H_e$,
turbines), and head *lost* ($H_L$, friction and fittings). Nothing else.
It is the single most-used equation in hydraulic engineering, and the
rest of this course keeps it within arm's reach.

2. From 4.1's checklist: which assumption does a long, real pipe violate?

**Look ahead**

1. Where does "lost" head actually go? (Energy is conserved — so what gives?)
2. What are the EGL and HGL, and what can you diagnose by *looking* at them?
3. Why does the kinetic-energy term wear an $\alpha$?

## Bernoulli, with a budget for reality

Run the energy version of the Reynolds Transport Theorem over a control
volume with one inlet (1) and one outlet (2) — steady, incompressible —
and after honest bookkeeping it lands here:

$$\frac{p_1}{\rho g}+\frac{\alpha_1}{2g}U_1^2 + z_1+H_\text{a}=
\frac{p_2}{\rho g}+\frac{\alpha_2}{2g}U_2^2 + z_2+H_\text{e}+H_\text{L}.$$

Everything is a height — industry standard, and not by accident: water
supply lives on elevation changes, so heads are the intuitive currency.
(A pump datasheet says "40 m", not "392 kPa," for the same reason
altimeters don't read pascals.) Three annotations:

**$H_L$ — where the "loss" goes.** Energy is conserved; *mechanical*
energy is not. Friction converts organized pressure/kinetic/potential
energy into disorganized thermal energy — the water gets warmer, by an
amount so small you'll never feel it (a 40 m head loss warms water less
than 0.1 °C) yet so hydraulically expensive it dominates Unit 8. "Loss"
is bookkeeping slang for *mechanical energy converted to heat, one-way*.

**$\alpha$ — the honest kinetic term.** The KE flux through a section
depends on the profile's shape ($u^3$-weighted), not just the average
speed. $\alpha$ patches the difference: exactly 2 for a laminar parabola,
about 1.05 for a blunt turbulent profile, 1 for a uniform stream or a
reservoir surface. The toolbox defaults $\alpha = 1$; you now know
precisely what that neglects and when to override it (`alpha1=`,
`alpha2=` in `PipeSystem` — a laminar oil line discharging as a jet is
the case that bites).

**$H_a$, $H_e$ — the machines.** A pump is a head *deposit* on the left;
a turbine a *withdrawal* on the right. What sets their size at a given
flow is the machines' own physics — Unit 8 uses their curves; Unit 10
opens them up.

## Grade lines: the equation as a picture

Plot two running totals along the pipe: the **EGL** (energy grade line,
all three heads) and the **HGL** (hydraulic grade line, EGL minus the
velocity head — physically, the height water would stand in a standpipe
tapped there). Now the equation becomes something you can *read*, the
same way 6.2 read profiles:

```{pyodide}
#| autorun: true
#| edit: false
#| echo: false
w = water(20)
Q = 0.012
p1 = Pipe(L=40, D=0.08, roughness='commercial_steel')
p2 = Pipe(L=60, D=0.08, roughness='commercial_steel')
pump_H = 18.0
hl1, hl2 = p1.head_loss(Q, w), p2.head_loss(Q, w)
U = Q/(np.pi*0.04**2); hv = U**2/(2*9.81)
x = [0, 40, 40, 100]
EGL = [10, 10-hl1, 10-hl1+pump_H, 10-hl1+pump_H-hl2]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4))
ax.plot(x, EGL, lw=2.5, color='crimson', label='EGL')
ax.plot(x, [e-hv for e in EGL], lw=2, ls='--', color='steelblue', label='HGL = EGL − U²/2g')
ax.axhline(0, color='k', lw=0.8)
ax.annotate('friction slope\n(module 8.2 prices it)', (18, 9.0), fontsize=9)
ax.annotate('the pump:\na vertical deposit H_a', (41, 14), fontsize=9)
ax.annotate('steeper?\nsame pipe — why?', (72, 21.5), fontsize=9, color='gray')
ax.set_xlabel('distance along pipe (m)'); ax.set_ylabel('head (m)')
ax.legend(loc='lower right'); ax.grid(alpha=0.3)
ax.set_title('a pumped line, read as grade lines (spoiler: the gray question is a trick)')
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
print(f"friction slopes: {hl1/40*1000:.2f} vs {hl2/60*1000:.2f} m per km — "
      "same pipe, same Q, same slope. Trust the ledger over the eyeball.")
```

The reading rules: EGL always falls in the flow direction (except at
machines — a pump is a vertical jump up, a turbine a drop); its *slope*
is the friction rate; the EGL–HGL gap is the velocity head (constant in
constant pipe, widening at a nozzle); and — the diagnostic with teeth —
**where the HGL dips below the pipe's elevation, the pressure there is
sub-atmospheric.** That's where a leaky joint sucks air *in* instead of
spraying water out, and where module 8.4's villain, cavitation, scouts
for a home.

::: {.callout-important}
## The misconception to leave behind
"Head loss means energy is destroyed" — no; and its cousin "the loss
comes back if the pipe widens again" — also no. Mechanical → thermal is a
one-way street (the second law's street). Contrast this with the
*velocity head*, which is fully refundable: slow the flow down gently and
pressure returns (the venturi's diffuser, 4.2). Distinguishing the
refundable from the irreversible is most of hydraulic literacy.
:::

## Earn it — 2 quick gates

The head equation with money attached: a pump lifts 25 L/s through 30 m of head at 70% efficiency. Ungraded; hints after a miss; **Show me** after two. Arguing about a gate with a classmate is the assignment, not a violation.

```{=html}
<div class="fl-reveal-all"></div>
```

```{=html}
<div class="fl-checkpoint"
     data-prompt="Shaft power the motor must supply?"
     data-answer="10.5" data-tol="0.03" data-units="kW"
     data-hint="P = ρgQH/η — the fluid takes ρgQH; the η under the bar is the machine's cut."
     data-solution="P = 998 × 9.81 × 0.025 × 30 / 0.7 = 10.5 kW."
     data-target="ee-s2"></div>
```

::: {#ee-s2 .fl-hidden}
And when head is *lost* instead of added, the energy doesn't vanish — it hides as heat:

```{=html}
<div class="fl-checkpoint"
     data-prompt="A pipeline loses 12 m of head to friction. Temperature rise of the water (c = 4186 J/kg·K)?"
     data-answer="0.028" data-tol="0.03" data-units="°C"
     data-hint="ΔT = g·h_L/c — the loss per kilogram is g·h_L joules, and water is a very deep thermal bucket."
     data-solution="ΔT = 9.81 × 12/4186 = 0.028 °C. Undetectable by hand, nonzero by law — Joule chased exactly this on his honeymoon."></div>
```

Head added has a motor bill; head lost has a thermometer receipt. The ledger always closes.

:::

## Check yourself

<details><summary>**Q1.** A horizontal, constant-diameter pipe carries steady flow with no machines. What does the head equation say the pressure does — and what does the HGL look like?</summary>
$\Delta z = 0$, KE terms cancel → $p$ falls by exactly $\rho g H_L$. The
HGL slopes straight down at the friction rate; the EGL parallels it one
velocity head above.
</details>

<details><summary>**Q2.** A turbine extracts 25 m of head from a flow of 2 m³/s of water. What power is that, before efficiency?</summary>
$P = \rho g Q H_e \approx 998 \times 9.81 \times 2 \times 25 \approx
490$ kW. Heads convert to watts through $\rho g Q$ — the same conversion
prices pump bills in Unit 8.
</details>

<details><summary>**Q3.** Between two points, water flows *uphill* while its pressure *rises*. No pump in between. Is this possible?</summary>
Only if the velocity head fell by more than both gains combined — a
widening pipe decelerating the flow (a diffuser). The three currencies
can each move either way; only the *total* (minus $H_L$) must fall.
</details>
